topic: GCP and the multi-cloud Rosetta stone
why: An FDE does not choose the customer's cloud; the customer's procurement team did that three years ago, and the next engagement will be on GCP or Azure with an AWS-shaped design in your head. The job in the first week is to translate fast and correctly: the customer's platform team says 'project', 'service account', 'Shared VPC', 'Container Apps environment' and you must map each to the AWS primitive you already know, and, more importantly, know exactly where the analogy lies to you (global VPCs, no deny-by-default, projects as API and billing boundaries). Deploying the same Dokeo container to Cloud Run with proper identity, secrets and networking is the fastest way to earn that fluency, and it is also the fastest path to a working demo in a customer GCP org where you have no EKS.
prerequisites: AWS mental model from 'AWS networking and compute' (topic 13) and 'AWS data' (topic 14): VPC, subnets, SG vs NACL, ALB, EC2, Lambda, RDS, S3, ElastiCache. This topic is a translation exercise, so the source language must be solid.

IAM policy evaluation, roles, and OIDC federation (IRSA, GitHub OIDC) from 'IAM and cloud security' (topic 15). GCP service accounts and Workload Identity Federation only make sense against that background.
Terraform state, providers, modules and `terraform import` from 'Terraform' (topic 12); you will write the google provider equivalents of resources you already wrote for AWS.

A hardened, non-root, multi-stage Dokeo image from 'Production images and supply chain' (topic 6), because Cloud Run's container contract (listen on `$PORT`, 10-second SIGTERM grace) surfaces every shortcut you took there.
The EKS cluster design from topic 16 (node groups, IRSA, ingress, cert-manager), so the GKE Autopilot and Workload Identity comparison lands.
A GCP account with billing enabled (the free trial credit is enough), `gcloud` installed, and a GitHub repo for Dokeo with a working CI job.

subtopics.name: Resource hierarchy: org, folders, projects, billing accounts
subtopics.learn: Know that GCP's unit of isolation is the project, not the account: every resource lives in exactly one project, IAM and org policies inherit org -> folder -> project -> resource, and a billing account is a separate resource linked to N projects. Distinguish project ID (immutable, globally unique, used in URLs and `--project`), project number (used in service-agent emails and Workload Identity principals) and display name. Practise `gcloud projects create dokeo-lab-$RANDOM --set-as-default`, `gcloud billing projects link PROJECT --billing-account=XXXXXX-XXXXXX-XXXXXX`, and understand that APIs are off until `gcloud services enable run.googleapis.com artifactregistry.googleapis.com secretmanager.googleapis.com sqladmin.googleapis.com`, which has no AWS equivalent (AWS services are always on; Azure needs resource-provider registration `az provider register`). Map: AWS Organization/OU/account and Azure management group/subscription/resource group; note that a GCP project is closer to an AWS account than to a resource group, and that nothing in GCP behaves like an Azure resource group as a deletion unit.

resource.label: Resource Manager docs: Resource hierarchy

subtopics.name: gcloud configurations and Application Default Credentials
subtopics.learn: Separate the two credential paths: `gcloud auth login` authorises the CLI itself, `gcloud auth application-default login` writes `~/.config/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json` that client libraries and Terraform read. Know the ADC lookup order: `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` env var -> the gcloud ADC file -> the attached service account via the metadata server (`http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/`, header `Metadata-Flavor: Google`) on GCE, GKE, Cloud Run. Use `gcloud config configurations create customer-x` / `activate` to keep customer projects separate (`gcloud config list` shows `account`, `project`, `compute/region`, `run/region`), and set a quota project with `gcloud auth application-default set-quota-project` when you hit `403 ... consumer project not found` from client libraries. Print tokens for debugging: `gcloud auth print-access-token` (OAuth2 access token, for Google APIs) and `gcloud auth print-identity-token` (OIDC ID token, for invoking Cloud Run). Map to `~/.aws/credentials` profiles plus the SDK credential chain and to `az login` / `az account set --subscription`.

resource.label: Google Cloud docs: Application Default Credentials

subtopics.name: IAM model: allow policies, roles, inheritance, and how it differs from AWS and Azure
subtopics.learn: Understand that GCP IAM is a set of allow policies attached to resources, each a list of bindings `{role, members[], condition?}`, where a role is a named bundle of permissions shaped `service.resource.verb` (e.g. `run.services.create`). Policies are evaluated as a union up the hierarchy: a binding at the folder grants on every project below and cannot be narrowed lower down; there is no implicit deny mechanism in allow policies (IAM Deny policies exist but are a separate, rarely used layer). Know the three role kinds and when to refuse each: basic (`roles/owner`, `roles/editor`, `roles/viewer`; too broad, and `editor` is what the default compute SA gets), predefined (`roles/run.admin`, `roles/run.invoker`, `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor`, `roles/cloudsql.client`, `roles/artifactregistry.reader`), and custom. Run `gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT --member=serviceAccount:dokeo-run@PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com --role=roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` and read the result with `gcloud projects get-iam-policy PROJECT --format=json`; use Policy Troubleshooter for 'why is this 403'. Contrast with AWS (identity policies plus resource policies plus SCPs plus permission boundaries, explicit deny beats allow) and Azure (role assignment = role definition + principal + scope, with deny assignments only from managed apps).

resource.label: IAM docs: IAM overview

subtopics.name: Service accounts, impersonation and Workload Identity Federation
subtopics.learn: A GCP service account wears two hats: it is an identity that holds roles, and it is a resource that other principals need `roles/iam.serviceAccountUser` (to act as it when deploying) or `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` (to mint tokens as it). Create `gcloud iam service-accounts create dokeo-run --display-name='Dokeo Cloud Run runtime'` and never deploy Cloud Run with the default compute SA (`PROJECT_NUMBER-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com`, historically project Editor). Prefer impersonation over keys: `gcloud --impersonate-service-account=SA ...` or `gcloud config set auth/impersonate_service_account SA`, and expect enterprise orgs to enforce `constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation`. For external identities use Workload Identity Federation: a pool, an OIDC provider with `--issuer-uri`, attribute mapping (`google.subject=assertion.sub`, `attribute.repository=assertion.repository`) and an attribute condition, then grant `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser` to `principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/NUM/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/POOL/attribute.repository/OWNER/REPO` on the SA. Map: SA = IAM role plus its trust policy (AWS) and managed identity plus federated identity credential (Azure); WIF = the IAM OIDC identity provider.

resource.label: IAM docs: Workload Identity Federation

subtopics.name: Networking Rosetta: global VPC, regional subnets, firewall rules, NAT, Private Google Access
subtopics.learn: Internalise the one structural difference that breaks AWS intuition: a GCP VPC is global and its subnets are regional, so a single VPC spans us-central1 and europe-west1 with internal routing and no peering. Firewall rules are VPC-scoped, stateful, have direction, priority (0-65535, lower wins) and targets (all instances, network tags, or service accounts); the implied rules are deny-all ingress and allow-all egress, and hierarchical firewall policies at org or folder level can override you. There is no NACL. Egress from private instances needs Cloud NAT on a Cloud Router; reaching `*.googleapis.com` from private subnets needs Private Google Access on the subnet. Managed services like Cloud SQL private IP live behind Private Services Access (an allocated range plus a VPC peering) or Private Service Connect; peering is non-transitive, and Shared VPC (host project owns the network, service projects attach workloads) is what enterprises actually run. Cloud Run has no VPC by default and reaches private IPs only via Direct VPC egress or a Serverless VPC Access connector. Map each to AWS (regional VPC, AZ subnets, route tables, IGW/NAT GW per AZ, SG stateful, NACL stateless, PrivateLink) and Azure (regional VNet, NSG at subnet or NIC with priority, NAT Gateway, Private Endpoint).

resource.label: VPC docs: Virtual Private Cloud overview

subtopics.name: Compute and serverless Rosetta: using the official comparison table critically
subtopics.learn: Work through the compute, containers and serverless rows of Google's own AWS/Azure/GCP comparison and annotate each with an analogy strength (exact / close / misleading). Compute Engine vs EC2 vs Azure VMs is exact, but note GCP machine families (e2, n2, c3, t2d), zonal placement and automatic sustained-use discounts that AWS and Azure do not have. Managed instance groups vs Auto Scaling groups vs VM Scale Sets is close; regional MIGs spread zones automatically. Cloud Run vs Fargate/App Runner vs Container Apps is where people get burned: Cloud Run bills per request-second and scales to zero, Fargate tasks do not scale to zero, App Runner is the closest AWS analogue, and Container Apps sits on KEDA with revision semantics very like Cloud Run. Cloud Run functions (formerly Cloud Functions) vs Lambda vs Azure Functions is close, GKE vs EKS vs AKS is close, App Engine vs Elastic Beanstalk vs App Service is close, Cloud Run jobs vs ECS scheduled tasks or Fargate one-off tasks is close. Write these rows into your one-page service map with the gotcha for each.

resource.label: Google Cloud docs: AWS, Azure and Google Cloud service comparison

subtopics.name: Artifact Registry: repos, auth, image paths, scanning, cleanup
subtopics.learn: Create a regional Docker repo with `gcloud artifacts repositories create dokeo --repository-format=docker --location=us-central1`, wire Docker auth with `gcloud auth configure-docker us-central1-docker.pkg.dev` (adds a `credHelpers` entry in `~/.docker/config.json`), and push as `us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT/dokeo/dokeo:GIT_SHA`. On Apple Silicon build with `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64` or Cloud Run's revision log will show `exec format error`. List and inspect with `gcloud artifacts docker images list REPO_PATH --include-tags` and, with `containerscanning.googleapis.com` enabled, `gcloud artifacts docker images describe IMAGE@sha256:... --show-package-vulnerability`. Add a cleanup policy that deletes untagged images older than 30 days and keeps the last 10 tagged versions. Know that pulling from Cloud Run in the same project works automatically but cross-project needs `roles/artifactregistry.reader` on the Cloud Run service agent `service-PROJECT_NUMBER@serverless-robot-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com`, and that a remote repository proxying Docker Hub is the fix for a customer hitting Hub rate limits. Map to ECR (`aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS`, 12-hour tokens, lifecycle policies) and ACR (`az acr login`, `AcrPull`).

resource.label: Artifact Registry docs: Pushing and pulling Docker images

subtopics.name: Cloud Run container contract and the first Dokeo deploy
subtopics.learn: Read the contract before deploying: the container must listen on `0.0.0.0` on the port in `$PORT` (default 8080; uvicorn's default host `127.0.0.1` fails the startup probe), must start listening within the startup timeout (default 240 s, TCP probe on `$PORT` unless you define an HTTP startup probe), gets SIGTERM and 10 seconds before SIGKILL, has an in-memory filesystem that counts against memory, and receives `K_SERVICE`, `K_REVISION`, `K_CONFIGURATION` env vars. Deploy Dokeo with `gcloud run deploy dokeo --image us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT/dokeo/dokeo:SHA --region us-central1 --service-account dokeo-run@PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com --no-allow-unauthenticated --port 8080 --cpu 1 --memory 512Mi --timeout 300 --max-instances 10 --execution-environment gen2` and read `gcloud run services describe dokeo --format yaml` to see the Knative-shaped spec underneath. When it fails, `gcloud run revisions list` and the revision's logs tell you which of the contract rules you broke; 'failed to start and listen on the port defined by the PORT environment variable' is almost always host binding, port, or a crash at import time. Map: an ECS Fargate task definition plus service plus ALB target group collapsed into one command, or `az containerapp up`.

resource.label: Cloud Run docs: Container runtime contract

subtopics.name: Cloud Run autoscaling, concurrency, CPU allocation and cold starts
subtopics.learn: Cloud Run scales instances on in-flight requests against `--concurrency` (default 80, max 1000) and CPU utilisation (target 60%), so the concurrency value is a statement about your app: a single-process async FastAPI can take 80, a sync WSGI worker should be set to 1 per worker. CPU is throttled to near zero between requests unless you set `--no-cpu-throttling` (CPU always allocated), which is why `BackgroundTasks` or `asyncio.create_task` work you kick off after returning the response silently never finishes. Fight cold starts with `--min-instances 1` (billed at idle rate), `--cpu-boost` for startup, a small image, and lazy imports; cap blast radius with `--max-instances` so a traffic spike cannot open 1,000 Postgres connections. Understand that idle instances live up to 15 minutes and that each instance is billed only while serving unless min-instances or always-on CPU is set. Map to Lambda reserved and provisioned concurrency, ECS service min/max tasks with target-tracking, and Container Apps min/max replicas with KEDA HTTP scaling rules.

resource.label: Cloud Run docs: About instance autoscaling

subtopics.name: Secrets, environment and configuration on Cloud Run
subtopics.learn: Store `DATABASE_URL` and API keys in Secret Manager (`gcloud secrets create dokeo-database-url --replication-policy=automatic`, `printf '%s' "$URL" | gcloud secrets versions add dokeo-database-url --data-file=-`), grant the runtime SA `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` on the secret (not the project), and inject with `--set-secrets=DATABASE_URL=dokeo-database-url:latest` as an env var or `--set-secrets=/secrets/db=dokeo-database-url:latest` as a file. Both are resolved when the instance starts, so a rotation with `latest` gives new instances a different value from running ones; pin a numeric version in production and roll a new revision to rotate. Use `--set-env-vars`, `--update-env-vars` and `--remove-env-vars` (each deploy or update creates a new revision), and know `--env-vars-file` for YAML. A missing `secretAccessor` shows up as the revision failing to start with a permission error on the secret, not as an app error. Map: ECS task definition `secrets` from Secrets Manager or SSM with the task execution role, and Container Apps secrets with Key Vault references via managed identity.

resource.label: Cloud Run docs: Configure secrets for services

subtopics.name: Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL from Cloud Run: sockets, connectors, private IP, IAM auth
subtopics.learn: Create `gcloud sql instances create dokeo-pg --database-version=POSTGRES_16 --tier=db-custom-1-3840 --region=us-central1` and know the three connection paths from Cloud Run: the built-in Cloud SQL connection (`--add-cloudsql-instances PROJECT:REGION:INSTANCE`, runtime SA needs `roles/cloudsql.client`, socket appears at `/cloudsql/PROJECT:REGION:INSTANCE`, so `DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:pw@/dokeo?host=/cloudsql/PROJECT:REGION:INSTANCE`); the Cloud SQL Python Connector library with IAM database authentication (`roles/cloudsql.instanceUser`, the SA becomes a Postgres user named like its email without `.gserviceaccount.com`); or private IP over Direct VPC egress (`--network --subnet --vpc-egress private-ranges-only`) which needs Private Services Access on the VPC. Compute the connection budget: max instances times pool size must stay under the instance's `max_connections`, or you will see `FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved` at the first scale-out. Know that Cloud SQL HA is a regional primary with a synchronous standby in another zone (like RDS Multi-AZ, not Aurora), read replicas can be cross-region, and maintenance windows matter. Map to RDS Proxy plus Secrets Manager and to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server with Entra authentication.

resource.label: Cloud SQL docs: Connect from Cloud Run

subtopics.name: Cloud Run authentication, ID tokens, ingress and load balancers
subtopics.learn: A service deployed with `--no-allow-unauthenticated` requires the caller to hold `roles/run.invoker` and to present an OIDC ID token whose `aud` is the service URL: `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-identity-token)" https://dokeo-XXXX-uc.a.run.app/health`. Service-to-service, the caller fetches a token from its own metadata server: `GET http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/identity?audience=https://dokeo-XXXX-uc.a.run.app` with `Metadata-Flavor: Google`, and the callee's IAM has the caller's SA bound to `run.invoker` via `gcloud run services add-iam-policy-binding`. Distinguish 401 (no or invalid token) from 403 (valid token, missing invoker). Making a service public with `--allow-unauthenticated` binds `allUsers` to `run.invoker` and fails in most enterprise orgs with 'users named in the policy do not belong to a permitted customer' because of Domain Restricted Sharing; the answer is not an org-policy exception but a Global external Application Load Balancer with a serverless NEG, Cloud Armor and IAP in front, with `--ingress internal-and-cloud-load-balancing` so the run.app URL is unreachable directly. Map to ALB with Cognito or Lambda function URLs with IAM auth, and to Container Apps built-in auth (Easy Auth).

resource.label: Cloud Run docs: Authentication overview

subtopics.name: Revisions, traffic splitting, tags and rollback
subtopics.learn: Every deploy or config change produces an immutable revision (`dokeo-00007-abc`) and traffic routes across revisions by percentage. Practise a canary: `gcloud run deploy dokeo --image ... --no-traffic --tag canary` gives a tagged URL `https://canary---dokeo-XXXX-uc.a.run.app` you can smoke-test with zero user traffic, then `gcloud run services update-traffic dokeo --to-tags canary=10`, then `--to-latest`. Roll back with `gcloud run services update-traffic dokeo --to-revisions dokeo-00006-xyz=100` in seconds without a rebuild. Know that env var, secret, CPU and concurrency changes also create revisions, so an operator 'just tweaking memory' has shifted 100% of traffic to a new revision. Map: Lambda aliases with weighted routing, ECS blue/green via CodeDeploy, and Container Apps multiple-revision mode with traffic weights and labels.

resource.label: Cloud Run docs: Rollbacks, gradual rollouts and traffic migration

subtopics.name: GKE vs EKS vs AKS: Autopilot, Workload Identity, ingress and release channels
subtopics.learn: Map the EKS design from topic 16 onto GKE: Standard mode (node pools = managed node groups) versus Autopilot (Google manages nodes, you pay for pod requests, privileged pods and hostPath are blocked, and it is the default for new clusters). Regional clusters replicate the control plane across three zones; zonal clusters do not. Workload Identity Federation for GKE is IRSA's cousin: annotate the KSA with `iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account` and bind `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser` to `serviceAccount:PROJECT.svc.id.goog[NS/KSA]`, or skip the SA entirely and grant roles directly to `principal://iam.googleapis.com/projects/NUM/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/PROJECT.svc.id.goog/subject/ns/NS/sa/KSA`. GKE Ingress and Gateway API provision the global external Application Load Balancer with container-native load balancing through NEGs, so there is no equivalent of the AWS Load Balancer Controller to install. Release channels (Rapid, Regular, Stable) auto-upgrade control plane and nodes, and `gcloud container clusters get-credentials` needs the `gke-gcloud-auth-plugin`. On AKS the analogues are node pools, Microsoft Entra Workload ID, Application Gateway for Containers and a free control-plane tier.

resource.label: GKE docs: About Workload Identity Federation for GKE

subtopics.name: Data Rosetta: Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Spanner, Firestore, Memorystore, Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Pub/Sub
subtopics.learn: Fill the data rows of the service map with the gotchas that matter to Dokeo. Cloud SQL = RDS = Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server (close); AlloyDB = Aurora PostgreSQL (close); Spanner has no exact analogue (Aurora DSQL and Cosmos DB are the nearest); Firestore = DynamoDB = Cosmos DB NoSQL (close, but Firestore is document-shaped, not single-table); Bigtable = DynamoDB/Keyspaces at scale; Memorystore = ElastiCache = Azure Cache for Redis (exact). Cloud Storage = S3 = Blob: bucket names are global, prefer uniform bucket-level access over ACLs, storage classes STANDARD/NEARLINE/COLDLINE/ARCHIVE carry minimum-storage durations of 0/30/90/365 days and retrieval fees, and V4 signed URLs need a private key or `--impersonate-service-account` with `iam.serviceAccounts.signBlob`; use `gcloud storage cp` (gsutil is legacy). BigQuery = Athena/Redshift Serverless = Synapse/Fabric: on-demand pricing by bytes scanned, so partition and cluster or a `SELECT *` dashboard costs real money. Pub/Sub = SNS+SQS (one product does fan-out and queueing; ordering keys and exactly-once are opt-in) = Service Bus/Event Hubs; Dataflow = Kinesis Data Analytics/Glue streaming = Stream Analytics.

resource.label: Cloud Storage docs: Storage classes

subtopics.name: Observability Rosetta: structured logs, trace correlation, Cloud Monitoring
subtopics.learn: Cloud Run ships stdout and stderr to Cloud Logging and parses one-JSON-object-per-line: emit `severity` (`DEBUG`..`CRITICAL`, not `level`), `message`, and `logging.googleapis.com/trace` set to `projects/PROJECT/traces/TRACE_ID` where TRACE_ID comes from the incoming `traceparent` or `X-Cloud-Trace-Context: TRACE_ID/SPAN_ID;o=1` header, so container logs nest under the request log in Logs Explorer. Query from the shell: `gcloud logging read 'resource.type="cloud_run_revision" AND resource.labels.service_name="dokeo" AND severity>=ERROR' --freshness=1h --limit=50 --format=json`; request logs live in `run.googleapis.com/requests`. Know the built-in metrics you will graph in the first customer review (`run.googleapis.com/request_count`, `request_latencies`, `container/instance_count`, `container/cpu/utilizations`), how log-based metrics and alerting policies work, and that ingestion costs about $0.50/GiB beyond the free 50 GiB, so a chatty DEBUG revision needs an exclusion filter in the Log Router. Error Reporting groups stack traces automatically. Map to CloudWatch log groups via the `awslogs` driver, Logs Insights, X-Ray with `X-Amzn-Trace-Id`, and to Azure Monitor Log Analytics KQL (`ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL`) plus Application Insights.

resource.label: Cloud Run docs: Logging and viewing logs

subtopics.name: Terraform google provider: Cloud Run v2, IAM footguns, project services, GCS backend
subtopics.learn: Rewrite the Dokeo deploy as Terraform: `provider "google" { project, region }` authenticating via ADC or `impersonate_service_account`; `google_project_service` for each API with `disable_on_destroy = false`; `google_artifact_registry_repository`; `google_service_account`; `google_secret_manager_secret` plus `_version`; `google_cloud_run_v2_service` with `template { service_account, scaling { min_instance_count, max_instance_count }, containers { image, env { value_source { secret_key_ref } } }, vpc_access { network_interfaces } }` and `ingress = "INGRESS_TRAFFIC_INTERNAL_LOAD_BALANCER"`; and `google_cloud_run_v2_service_iam_member` for `roles/run.invoker`. Learn the IAM trio by heart: `google_project_iam_policy` is authoritative for the whole project and will delete the customer's existing bindings including service agents, `google_project_iam_binding` is authoritative for one role, `google_project_iam_member` is additive and is the safe default. Use `backend "gcs" { bucket, prefix }` (locking is built in), expect IAM eventual consistency after creating an SA (a `time_sleep` of 30 s or a retry is the pragmatic fix), and add `lifecycle { ignore_changes = [template[0].containers[0].image, client, client_version] }` when CI deploys images outside Terraform so plans stay clean.

resource.label: Terraform Registry: google_cloud_run_v2_service

subtopics.name: The Azure column: Entra ID, subscriptions, resource groups, managed identity, Container Apps
subtopics.learn: Learn just enough Azure to fill the third column honestly. Hierarchy: Entra ID tenant -> management groups -> subscriptions -> resource groups -> resources, where the resource group is a lifecycle and deletion unit with no GCP or AWS equivalent. RBAC is role definition + principal + scope, with Owner/Contributor/Reader built in and the classic trap that Contributor cannot create role assignments (you need Owner or User Access Administrator). Managed identity (system-assigned or user-assigned) is the SA or IAM role, and a federated identity credential on it is WIF or the OIDC provider. Run the third deploy: `az login`, `az account set --subscription ID`, `az group create -n rg-dokeo -l eastus`, `az acr create`, `az acr login`, then `az containerapp up --name dokeo --resource-group rg-dokeo --image ACR.azurecr.io/dokeo:SHA --ingress external --target-port 8080` and note what it created for you: a Container Apps environment backed by a Log Analytics workspace, a revision, and an external ingress. Container Apps scales with KEDA rules, has single or multiple revision mode with traffic weights, and reads secrets from Key Vault through the managed identity. Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server, Azure Cache for Redis, Blob Storage and Azure Monitor complete the row.

resource.label: Microsoft Learn: AWS to Azure services comparison

subtopics.name: Day-one reconnaissance: org policies, Cloud Asset Inventory, regions and zones, quotas
subtopics.learn: Before your first deploy in a customer org, inventory and list what will block you. Inventory: `gcloud projects list --filter='lifecycleState:ACTIVE'`, `gcloud services list --enabled --project P`, and with `roles/cloudasset.viewer` run `gcloud asset search-all-resources --scope=organizations/ORG --asset-types='run.googleapis.com/Service,sqladmin.googleapis.com/Instance,container.googleapis.com/Cluster' --format='table(name,location,project)'` and `gcloud asset search-all-iam-policies --scope=projects/P --query='policy:roles/owner'` to see who holds Owner and which SAs have keys (AWS: Resource Explorer, Config aggregators; Azure: `az graph query -q "Resources | summarize count() by type"`). Blockers: `gcloud resource-manager org-policies list --project P` and read `constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation`, `constraints/iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains` (Domain Restricted Sharing, kills `allUsers`), `constraints/gcp.resourceLocations`, `constraints/run.allowedIngress` and `constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess`; these are the analogue of AWS Service Control Policies and Azure Policy and, like SCPs, only restrict. Know the scope of every resource you touch: zonal (VMs, persistent disks, zonal GKE), regional (subnets, Cloud Run, Cloud SQL, regional MIGs), multi-regional or global (VPC, Cloud Storage multi-region, global load balancers). Quotas are per project per region and surface as HTTP 429 `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`; check with `gcloud compute regions describe us-central1` and the Quotas page, and request increases early because Cloud Run instance and CPU quotas in a fresh project are low (AWS: `aws service-quotas request-service-quota-increase`; Azure: the per-region vCPU family quota that blocks day-one VM creation).

resource.label: Resource Manager docs: Introduction to the Organization Policy Service

subtopics.name: Keyless CI: GitHub Actions to Cloud Run through Workload Identity Federation
subtopics.learn: Wire the Dokeo repo so no JSON key ever exists: the job declares `permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read }`, `google-github-actions/auth@v2` receives `workload_identity_provider: projects/NUM/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/github/providers/github` and either `service_account:` (impersonation) or nothing (direct WIF with roles granted to the `principalSet://`). Set `token_format: access_token` and feed `docker/login-action` with registry `us-central1-docker.pkg.dev`, username `oauth2accesstoken`, password `${{ steps.auth.outputs.access_token }}`, push by digest, then `google-github-actions/deploy-cloudrun@v2` with `service`, `region`, `image` (or `gcloud run deploy` after `setup-gcloud`). Lock the provider's attribute condition to `assertion.repository == 'OWNER/dokeo' && assertion.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` so a fork PR's token cannot deploy, and pin action versions by SHA as you did in topic 6. Compare line by line with `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` (`role-to-assume`, IAM OIDC provider `token.actions.githubusercontent.com`, `sub` condition in the trust policy) and `azure/login` (federated credential with subject `repo:OWNER/REPO:ref:refs/heads/main`, `client-id`, `tenant-id`, `subscription-id`).

resource.label: GitHub: google-github-actions/auth

outcomes: You can take a fresh GCP project with billing linked and, in under 30 minutes and without a service account key, have Dokeo running on Cloud Run behind `--no-allow-unauthenticated` with a dedicated runtime SA, `DATABASE_URL` from Secret Manager, a Cloud SQL connection via the `/cloudsql` socket, and a successful `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-identity-token)"` against `/health`.

You can produce a one-page service map of the roughly 25 services Dokeo and its pipeline touch across AWS, GCP and Azure, with an analogy-strength column (exact / close / misleading) and a one-line gotcha per row, and defend every 'misleading' entry (global VPC, scale-to-zero, resource groups, deny semantics) to a platform architect.

You can read a Cloud Run revision failure from `gcloud run revisions list` and the revision logs and name the cause within two minutes for each of: `exec format error` (arm64 image), listening on 127.0.0.1 or the wrong port, missing `secretmanager.secretAccessor`, missing `iam.serviceaccounts.actAs`, and `allUsers` blocked by Domain Restricted Sharing.

You can explain GCP IAM evaluation (allow-policy union up the hierarchy, no implicit deny, role kinds) next to AWS evaluation (explicit deny, SCPs, boundaries) and Azure RBAC (scope-based assignments), and answer 'who can read this bucket?' in each cloud with the actual command or console tool.

You can configure GitHub Actions to deploy to Cloud Run through Workload Identity Federation with an attribute condition pinned to repo and branch, and describe precisely what a compromised fork pull request could and could not do with that pipeline, then give the AWS OIDC and Azure federated-credential equivalents.

You can write the Terraform for Artifact Registry, runtime SA, secrets, `google_cloud_run_v2_service` and invoker IAM using only additive `_member` resources, and articulate to a customer why a colleague's `google_project_iam_policy` would have removed the project's service-agent bindings.

You can correlate a slow request across Cloud Run request logs and Dokeo's structured container logs by trace ID in Logs Explorer, reproduce the query with `gcloud logging read`, and translate it to a CloudWatch Logs Insights query and a KQL query.

You can walk into a customer GCP org and, within an hour, list active projects, enabled APIs, Cloud Run services, Owners and SA keys via Cloud Asset Inventory, and list the org policy constraints that will block your planned deployment, producing a short pre-kickoff landing-zone questionnaire.
failureModes: The image is built on an Apple Silicon laptop without `--platform linux/amd64`; the first Cloud Run revision dies with `exec format error`, the error is buried in the revision log rather than the deploy output, and the team spends an hour rewriting the Dockerfile CMD before anyone checks the architecture.

Dokeo starts uvicorn with its default host `127.0.0.1` and port 8000; Cloud Run's startup probe never connects and the deploy fails with 'container failed to start and listen on the port defined by the PORT environment variable' while the app itself is perfectly healthy in the logs.

Nobody sets `--service-account`, so the service runs as the default compute SA with project Editor; the customer's security review flags it a week before go-live, and the rushed switch to a scoped SA breaks the deploy because no one had listed which secrets, buckets and Cloud SQL instances the app actually reads.

A demo needs a public URL; `--allow-unauthenticated` fails with 'users named in the policy do not belong to a permitted customer' due to Domain Restricted Sharing, and the FDE files for an org-policy exception that takes two weeks instead of fronting the service with a load balancer and IAP or shipping an authenticated client.

A FastAPI endpoint returns 202 and does its work in a `BackgroundTask`; with CPU throttled between requests the task never completes, the customer sees rows stuck in 'processing' only in production, and it takes days to connect the symptom to CPU allocation rather than to the code.

Traffic spikes, Cloud Run scales to its default 100 instances, each with a 10-connection pool, and Cloud SQL rejects with `FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved`; the fix is `--max-instances`, a smaller pool or a connection proxy, but the first instinct is to resize the database instance.

An engineer 'cleans up' IAM with `google_project_iam_policy` in Terraform; the apply removes the Cloud Build and serverless robot service-agent bindings the customer's platform team had added by hand, every deploy in the project fails for the rest of the day, and the bindings have to be reconstructed from the Cloud Asset Inventory history.

A secret is referenced as `:latest`, the DBA rotates the password in Secret Manager without redeploying, and for the next hour new instances authenticate with the new password while long-lived instances still hold connections on the old one, so failures appear only at scale-out and look like flakiness.
interviewQuestions: A customer runs a workload on EKS with IRSA, RDS Postgres, S3 and an ALB, and asks you to stand up the same thing on GCP for a newly acquired business unit next quarter. Walk me through the service-by-service mapping, name the three places the analogy is misleading enough to change the design, and tell me what you would warn them about before they commit a date.

Trace a request from one Cloud Run service to another that is deployed with `--no-allow-unauthenticated`: where does the caller get its token, what fields does Cloud Run check, what IAM binding must exist, and how do you distinguish and debug a 401 from a 403? Then describe the equivalent flow between two services on ECS behind IAM-authenticated endpoints.

Design a CI pipeline that deploys the same container to Cloud Run, ECS and Azure Container Apps with zero long-lived credentials. Name the primitive in each cloud, the exact trust condition you would set, and what an attacker who lands code in a fork pull request could and could not do in each.

Dokeo on Cloud Run shows p50 of 40 ms and p99 of 3.5 s and the customer says 'GCP is slow'. Using only Cloud Run metrics and Cloud Logging, how do you prove or disprove that in 20 minutes, what are the four most likely causes, and what is the fix and cost of each?

A customer security lead says 'no public ingress and no service account keys, ever'. Design ingress for Dokeo on Cloud Run for internal employees and for a partner webhook under those constraints, and explain how Domain Restricted Sharing and `run.allowedIngress` interact with your design. What would the same design look like on AWS?

Terraform apply creates a runtime service account and its bindings, and thirty seconds later `gcloud run deploy --service-account` fails with `Permission 'iam.serviceaccounts.actAs' denied`. Give me the two most likely causes, how you would tell them apart, and how you make the pipeline robust to both.

Explain how GCP's allow-policy inheritance, AWS's explicit-deny evaluation and Azure's scope-based role assignments each answer the question 'can this principal read that object?', and describe a permission that is trivial to express in one of the three and awkward or impossible in another.
proofOfWork: A public repository, `dokeo-rosetta`, that a reviewer can run cold against three empty accounts. `make gcp` applies Terraform (project services, Artifact Registry, runtime SA, Secret Manager, Cloud SQL, `google_cloud_run_v2_service` with invoker IAM, all additive `_member` bindings) and ends with an authenticated `curl` against `/health` and a canary traffic split demonstrated with `gcloud run services update-traffic`; `make aws` deploys the same image to ECS Fargate behind an ALB using the topic 13 to 16 modules; `make azure` runs `az containerapp up` with a user-assigned managed identity and Key Vault secret. A single GitHub Actions workflow deploys to all three through OIDC (WIF, `configure-aws-credentials`, `azure/login`) with repo-and-branch-pinned trust conditions and SHA-pinned actions. The README holds the one-page service map with analogy-strength and gotcha columns, a side-by-side 'same failure, three clouds' table (wrong port, missing secret permission, public ingress blocked by policy) showing the exact error text in each cloud and the fix, and a twenty-question GCP landing-zone questionnaire (org policies in force, Shared VPC host project, allowed regions, SA key policy, Domain Restricted Sharing, egress path to Cloud SQL, logging sinks, quota ceilings) written to be sent to a customer platform team before the kickoff call.
